title: The origins of rodeo: a competitive sport

paragraphs.text: Rodeo is a sporting event testing the skills and speed of cowboys using horses, cows, and bulls. The beginnings of rodeo in the United States can be traced back to the early 1700s, when mounted horsemen from Spain, called ranchers, dominated the western US. These ranchers had a long tradition of horseriding and were expert at tasks that included roping, horse breaking, cattle driving, riding, and herding. In the early 1800s, people leaving the East coast and heading west came into contact with Spanish ranch culture and began to copy and adapt many of the techniques, styles and traditions developed over the previous 100 years.

American ranch culture was further developed during the long cattle drives needed to bring cows to market. In the first part of this journey, cattle were led by ranchers traveling over long distances from the ranches to departure points such as Kansas City. From Kansas City, trains would carry the cows east to busy cities like Chicago and Saint Louis, where they were sold. These cattle drives led to the development of the culture of American cowboys, who made their living on the many ranches and cattle trails. At the end of these long trails, groups of cowboys would often hold informal competitions among themselves to see who were the best riders and ropers. The first recorded rodeo-style event took place at this time.

Toward the end of the 1800s, much of the cowboy era came to an end with the construction of railroad lines throughout the west. There was no longer a need for long cattle drives and cowboys because trains were much faster. Instead, many cowboys began to take other jobs with what became a new American phenomenon, the Wild West Show. Entrepreneurs like the legendary Buffalo Bill Cody began to organize these Wild West Shows to make money by glamorizing and preserving the disappearing cowboy culture. He also acted in some of these shows but left the horse riding to his headline performers. The spectacle and showmanship of modern rodeo originated here.

At the same time, other cowboys were able to start making a living by competing in informal competitions - this time, these events attracted paying spectators, whose entrance fees were used as cash prizes for event winners. Small towns across the west would hold annual horse shows. These popular shows spread across the country and would outlast the Wild West Shows, which cost a lot of money to organize and produce. These cowboy competitions were typically referred to as 'rodeos'.

However, new guidelines were needed to standardize the events and protect the safety of the competitors. Many of the major rodeo committees came together in 1929 to agree on uniform rules of competition for this emerging sport of rodeo. The new organization was dubbed the Rodeo Association of America (RAA). It now became easier to determine the champions in each event based on commonly understood benchmarks. For example, for the rodeo event of bull riding, it was decided riders were allowed to hold the bull strap with only one hand, and had to ride the bull for at least eight seconds to receive a score from the judges.

Even with this new organization, cowboys competing individually in rodeos still faced many problems. The cowboys were often taken advantage of and money paid to event winners was often less than agreed upon. In 1936 a landmark moment happened when a group of roughly 60 cowboys at the Boston Garden Rodeo became angry with WT Johnson, a promoter who failed to advertise the rodeo and to pay them their share of the prize money. So they decided to stage a protest by refusing to compete. The event planners looked for replacements but were unsuccessful, so they finally gave the cowboys what they wanted. With a newfound sense of worth, the cowboys formed the Rodeo Cowboys Association (RCA), and the modern sport of rodeo was born. This is a sport that is largely governed by the participants in the sport, the cowboys. One decision the members made early on was to determine what winners would receive. As many RCA members were also boxers, the buckle, commonly awarded to the best boxers, became the preferred trophy of rodeo events.

In the modern era, rodeo has grown into a huge national sport. Membership of the RCA (now the PRCA, Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association) includes nearly 5,000 cowboys, from those who compete in professional rodeo for a living, criss-crossing the country with horses that they own, to those who only compete in rodeos close to home on the weekends. The business and sport of rodeo is now as legitimate as any other national sport, and the PRCA has achieved a status equal to the professional American football and basketball leagues.
